intro.uz: Biografik matn: Zahiriddin Muhammad Bobur — hukmdor, «Boburnoma» muallifi va shoir. Topshiriqlar: True/False/Not Given, test savollari (ishora, maqsad, xulosa) va gap toʻldirish (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS). Taxminan 20 daqiqa: sanalar va joy nomlarini (Andijon, Samarqand, Kobul, Panipat, Agra) matnda belgilab oling — savollarning koʻpi aynan shu tayanch nuqtalar atrofida tuzilgan.

paragraphs.en: Many rulers have founded empires, and a good number have commissioned flattering chronicles of their deeds. Rarely, however, has a ruler left behind a personal account as candid as the one written by Zahiriddin Muhammad Babur, the prince from the Fergana Valley who became the founder of the Mughal dynasty in India. His life story is remarkable in itself, a sequence of reversals in which kingdoms were won and lost with bewildering speed. What has secured his lasting reputation, though, is not only what he did but the way he wrote about it.

Babur was born in Andijan in 1483, the son of Umar Shaikh Mirza, who ruled the small principality of Fergana. Through his father he was descended from Amir Temur, and through his mother from Genghis Khan, a double lineage that conferred enormous prestige but also fuelled ambitions that his modest territory could hardly sustain. When his father died in an accident in 1494, Babur inherited the throne while still a boy of about eleven, surrounded by relatives and advisers whose loyalty could not be taken for granted.

The years that followed were dominated by a struggle for Samarkand, the former capital of Temur, whose possession represented for any Timurid prince the ultimate symbol of legitimacy. Babur captured the city more than once, yet on each occasion he proved unable to hold it. The decisive challenge came from Muhammad Shaybani Khan, whose forces were consolidating their power across the region. Driven out of Samarkand and eventually deprived of Fergana as well, Babur spent a period as a ruler without a realm, moving from place to place with a dwindling band of followers.

His fortunes changed in 1504, when he seized Kabul. The city gave him a secure base, and for two decades he ruled there, all the while looking for an opportunity to restore his position in Central Asia. A final attempt to retake Samarkand, made with the support of the Safavid Shah of Iran, briefly succeeded but ended in failure. Gradually, Babur's attention turned south-east, towards the wealthy lands of northern India, into which he led a series of expeditions.

In 1526, at Panipat, north of Delhi, his army confronted the forces of Ibrahim Lodi, the Sultan of Delhi, an army generally believed to have been far larger than his own. Babur's victory is often attributed to his skilful use of field fortifications and gunpowder weapons, which were still relatively uncommon on Indian battlefields. The battle laid the foundation of what became known as the Mughal Empire. Babur himself did not live long enough to consolidate it: he died in Agra in 1530, and his remains were later taken to Kabul, in keeping with his wishes. His descendants, however, would rule much of the subcontinent for generations, presiding over a culture of extraordinary richness.

It is the Boburnoma, known in English as the Baburnama, that gives Babur a place in literary as well as political history. Written in Chagatai Turkic, the literary language of the Timurid world, the memoir records his campaigns, but it does so with a frankness that is rare in royal writing. Babur admits defeats, errors of judgement and moments of despair, and he comments shrewdly, and sometimes harshly, on the character of allies and enemies alike. Equally striking is his curiosity. He describes the landscapes, fruits, birds and customs of Fergana, Kabul and India with the eye of a naturalist, and he is not above complaining that his new Indian domains lacked the melons and grapes of his homeland. The work was later translated into Persian at the court of his grandson Akbar, which helped it reach a wider audience.

Babur was also an accomplished poet. He composed ghazals and rubais in Turkic, and he is often ranked among the most significant poets to have written in Chagatai after Alisher Navoi. Many of his verses express longing for the homeland he had been forced to leave, a theme that lends them particular resonance for readers in Uzbekistan today. Soldier, ruler, memoirist and poet, Babur defies easy categorisation, and it is perhaps this very complexity that continues to draw readers to his work five centuries after it was written.

grammar.example: Rarely, however, has a ruler left behind a personal account as candid as the one written by Zahiriddin Muhammad Babur

title.uz: Sifatdosh oborot: Driven out of …, Babur spent …

grammar.example: Driven out of Samarkand and eventually deprived of Fergana as well, Babur spent a period as a ruler without a realm

questions.statement: Babur's family background gave him prestige but also encouraged ambitions beyond his resources.

explain.uz: «a double lineage that conferred enormous prestige but also fuelled ambitions that his modest territory could hardly sustain» — paraphrase.

questions.statement: Babur became ruler of Fergana as an adult.

explain.uz: «Babur inherited the throne while still a boy of about eleven».

questions.statement: Babur's final attempt on Samarkand, made with Safavid support, achieved no success at all.

explain.uz: «briefly succeeded but ended in failure» — qisqa muddat muvaffaqiyat boʻlgan, demak «no success at all» notoʻgʻri.

questions.statement: Babur was buried permanently in Agra, where he died.

explain.uz: «he died in Agra in 1530, and his remains were later taken to Kabul, in keeping with his wishes».

questions.statement: The Persian translation of the memoir was produced during Babur's lifetime.

explain.uz: «later translated into Persian at the court of his grandson Akbar» — nabirasi davrida, Bobur vafotidan keyin.

questions.statement: Babur learned to write poetry from a famous poet at his father's court.

explain.uz: G xatboshida Bobur shoir boʻlgani va Navoiydan keyingi yirik shoirlar qatorida turishi aytilgan, ammo kimdan oʻrgangani haqida maʼlumot yoʻq.

questions.prompt: In paragraph A, the writer suggests that Babur's lasting reputation depends mainly on
options: the size of the empire he founded
the flattering chronicles written about him
both his achievements and the way he recorded them
the speed with which he won his kingdoms

explain.uz: «What has secured his lasting reputation … is not only what he did but the way he wrote about it».

questions.prompt: In paragraph B, the phrase "a double lineage" refers to Babur's descent from
options: Umar Shaikh Mirza and the rulers of Fergana
two branches of the Timurid family in Samarkand

explain.uz: «Through his father he was descended from Amir Temur, and through his mother from Genghis Khan, a double lineage …» — ikki tomonlama nasab.

questions.prompt: Why was Samarkand so important to Babur?
options: It was the richest trading city in the region.
Controlling it confirmed a Timurid prince's right to rule.
It was the city where he had been born.
It provided a safe base for his expeditions to India.

explain.uz: «whose possession represented for any Timurid prince the ultimate symbol of legitimacy» — «legitimacy» = hokimiyatga qonuniy huquq. Tugʻilgan joyi — Andijon; xavfsiz baza — Kobul.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention Babur's complaint about melons and grapes?
options: to show that Indian agriculture was poorly developed
to illustrate the personal and unguarded tone of his observations
to explain why he decided to return to Kabul
to criticise his attitude towards the people of India

explain.uz: Bu misol «frankness» va «curiosity» haqidagi fikrni tasdiqlaydi; «he is not above complaining» — u hatto mayda shaxsiy noroziliklarini ham yashirmaydi.

questions.prompt: After 1504, Kabul provided Babur with a secure ___.

explain.uz: «The city gave him a secure base».

questions.prompt: At Panipat, Babur made skilful use of field fortifications and ___ weapons.

explain.uz: «his skilful use of field fortifications and gunpowder weapons».

questions.prompt: The Boburnoma was written in ___, the literary language of the Timurid world.

explain.uz: «Written in Chagatai Turkic, the literary language of the Timurid world».

questions.prompt: Many of Babur's poems express ___ for the homeland he had lost.

explain.uz: «Many of his verses express longing for the homeland he had been forced to leave».
